item.title: Who Is Jason Turkish, Haley Stevens’s Fiancé?
item.description:
Even before the Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens scrambled Michigan’s U.S. Senate race on Sunday by endorsing the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, another man in her orbit had garnered increased attention: Jason Turkish, her fiancé.

Mr. Turkish said last Wednesday that he would not support the Democratic Party’s nominee for U.S. Senate, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, over his criticisms of Israel. Then, on Sunday, Ms. Stevens threw her support behind Mr. Rogers after joining him for services at a prominent Black church in Detroit, despite previous assurances to Democratic leaders that she would support her party’s ticket.

The feud between Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed — and the role that Mr. Turkish may have played in the intraparty spat — underlines how the debate over U.S. support of Israel has roiled Democratic politics.

Here’s what else we know.

Mr. Turkish, 39, is a lawyer and fund-raiser for Democratic candidates and Jewish causes. He is based in Southfield, a suburb of Detroit, and graduated from the University of Michigan in 2007, the same year as Dr. El-Sayed. He is also the president and managing partner of Nyman Turkish, a disability rights firm. He has been legally blind since birth.

Mr. Turkish is a longtime political donor. A self-proclaimed “lifelong Democrat,” he and his firm have given money to multiple Democratic campaigns across the country but he has also donated to at least one Republican, Senator Susan Collins of Maine, according to federal records.

Former Gov. James Blanchard of Michigan, a close friend of Ms. Stevens’s, described Mr. Turkish as “a real political junkie” who has raised a lot of money for Democratic candidates in the state. He is also active in the state’s Jewish and pro-Israel circles and is a donor to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. He has relatives who live and were born in Israel.

Mr. Turkish and Ms. Stevens met after the 2022 midterm elections through a mutual friend. They bonded as they discussed her disability rights legislation, she said in interviews, and their conversations about policy evolved into a romantic relationship. They announced their engagement in August, shortly after Ms. Stevens lost the primary election to Dr. El-Sayed.

“We just fell in love,” Ms. Stevens told The Detroit News in August. “We had years of just friendship and conversation, and we have a lot of shared values and commitment to family and friends in Michigan.”

The couple vacationed in Italy and Israel after sharing the news of their engagement. Ms. Stevens has said she has met with a rabbi to discuss converting to Judaism before they get married next summer.

In the final week of the campaign, Mr. Turkish said he would vote for Mr. Rogers because he felt Dr. El-Sayed had not sufficiently moderated his views on Israel. Mr. Turkish attended an event for the Republican Jewish Coalition supporting Mr. Rogers shortly after endorsing him.

“I watched Haley graciously concede an election, and open her arms and her heart to Abdul on Aug. 5, the day after the primary, and I prayed that he would moderate, and he hasn’t,” he said in an interview before the event.

On Friday Mr. Turkish appeared on TMZ to explain his support for Mr. Rogers, pointing to a digital advertisement from supporters of Dr. El-Sayed that blames rising grocery prices in the United States on its support for Israel’s military campaign. He called on Dr. El-Sayed to disavow the ad and suggested that if he did not, Ms. Stevens would not support him. Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign sought to distance the candidate from the ad, saying that it was created by a left-wing political action committee, Rebellion PAC, and was “not affiliated in any way” with him or his candidacy.

On Sunday, when Ms. Stevens appeared alongside Mr. Rogers at the Perfecting Church in Detroit, Mr. Turkish was also in attendance.

item.title: Trump Says a Senator Has a ‘Powerful’ Rear. Will It Help Him Win?
item.description:
There it was. The most famous rear end in politics.

It was hard to see under layers of flannel and quilted vest, but that was definitely it.

The one that President Trump has called a “great ass” and a “pile of muscle.” The one that, as a result, starred on “Saturday Night Live” and blew up on TikTok. The one that belongs to Senator Jon Husted, the Republican candidate in a high-stakes election in Ohio, who for a brief moment at a campaign event on Saturday night turned around onstage.

“We couldn’t see it,” said Missy Hartman, 58, a baker at a grocery store.

“I never check anyone’s butt out,” said Jeff Bair, 73, a farmer.

“It’s a middle-aged ass,” said Karen Tetrick, 52, who owns an apartment complex. “I should know, I have one.”

Here is the thing about Mr. Trump’s comments about Mr. Husted’s rear: Online and across Ohio, they have more people talking about the senator than anyone has in the two years since he was appointed to the Senate to succeed Vice President JD Vance.

Mr. Trump, who first complimented the senator’s backside at a campaign rally last month and has not stopped talking about it since, can be mocking, crass and cruel with his focus of physicality. But in this case, he took a candidate who had toiled in relative anonymity and gave him an identity that stuck.

“I’m jealous,” Mr. Vance said last week on Fox News of Mr. Husted’s rump. “The president has never said that about me.”

Mr. Husted, 59, has leaned into the newfound attention. Before his physique — or rather, a description of his physique — went viral, even some hard-core Republican voters in Ohio had hardly heard of him. Many of them thought his opponent, Sherrod Brown, a Democrat and former senator who has been a fixture in Ohio politics since the 1970s, was still in office.

Now at least some of them know about Mr. Husted’s allegedly powerful glutes. What’s his secret? His staff members declined to share his gym routine. They also declined to let a reporter join him for a workout, citing “trade secrets.”

Mr. Trump has claimed the attention on Mr. Husted’s frame has given the senator a 12-point lift in the polls. A new New York Times and Siena University poll shows Mr. Brown, a longtime economic populist, ahead by six points.

“I know nothing about Jon Husted’s body,” said Judy Kruger, 68, a Republican. “It’s not anything to make me vote one way or another.”

Jason Vannette, 50, who on Friday joined a small group of Democratic protesters outside a rally in Toledo for Republican candidates, sized up Mr. Trump’s remarks this way: “It’s weird.”

For his part, Mr. Husted has played up the president’s commentary.

At the event on Saturday in Fairlawn, he arrived with a football in his hand and kept it with him as he took the microphone and addressed the crowd.

“During the campaign, President Trump discovered that I was a college football player,” said Mr. Husted, who played at the University of Dayton nearly 40 years ago. “He’s been talking about it.”

The senator threw the football into a room of attendees eating apple pie.

There was a reason Mr. Trump said he had been “studying” Mr. Husted’s body.

Republicans in Ohio are trying to turn the Senate race, which could decide control of the chamber, into a culture war much like the ones that delivered Mr. Trump and others on the right to power.

On one side, according to Mr. Husted: socialism, transgender athletes and a world in which Mother’s Day becomes “Birthing Person’s Day.”

On the other? In the words of the president, a former football player with “a big piece of muscle” on his backside.

“I don’t do this with men very often,” Mr. Trump said last month at a rally in Youngstown. “I started examining his body.”

He apparently would like to continue to do so aboard Air Force One. Bill Pulte, a top federal housing official, made a poster of Mr. Husted for the president to display on the plane.

So far, the focus on Mr. Husted’s buttocks appears to have mixed results in Ohio — or at least it did among the voters who convened on Sunday at a bar in Geneva to meet candidates and watch the Cleveland Browns game.

“Who cares?” said Donald Goodenow, 66, a lab tech wearing a Harley-Davidson sweatshirt, when a reporter asked him if he had heard Mr. Trump’s comments about Mr. Husted.

Mr. Goodenow said he thought Mr. Brown was in office and planned to vote for Mr. Husted because “by the looks of most of the Democratic Party, they’re out to lunch.”

Ms. Tetrick said she was considering leaving Mr. Husted’s bubble blank, despite broadly supporting Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.

“Sherrod Brown, I do appreciate him over the years — he did care about the people,” said Ms. Tetrick. “Husted, I just don’t know.”

Mr. Husted was not at the bar on Sunday with the other Republican candidates who had taken a bus to mingle with voters at the sports bar.

Perhaps he was at the gym.

Mack Liederman contributed from Toledo, Ohio.

]]>

item.title: In Run-Up to Midterms, Legacy of 2020 Looms Large Over Justice Dept.
item.description:
Senior leaders of the Justice Department, many of them veterans of President Trump’s legal and political wars over the past decade, share a singular, striking attribute: They have not admitted, unequivocally or plainly, that he lost the 2020 election.

Attorney General Todd Blanche; his predecessor, Pam Bondi; the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel; and Harmeet K. Dhillon, the head of the department’s civil rights division, have all avoided providing yes-or-no answers about the election in appearances before Congress. Instead, they have acknowledged only that President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory was legally certified.

Emil Bove III, a former Blanche aide, offered a telling non-answer during his confirmation process for a federal judgeship last year: It was inappropriate to opine on 2020 because it was an unresolved “political or policy debate,” he wrote in a questionnaire.

This refusal to acknowledge the fact that Mr. Trump lost, a go-to tactic for nominees seeking to avoid contradicting the president, has become so commonplace it no longer warrants much attention. Yet it reflects the enduring legacy of a polarizing election whose reverberations are still being felt, perhaps most consequentially in the department’s presumption that voter fraud is so rampant that it requires a forceful federal response. That premise has been challenged by state election officials and expert analysis.

“This is a different approach than we have seen in any previous Department of Justice, whether it was run by Republicans or Democrats,” said Karen Brinson Bell, the former executive director of the North Carolina State Board of Elections.

Ms. Brinson Bell said the administration’s current initiatives, like its attempt to curtail mail-in voting, the unsuccessful effort to obtain sensitive voter data from states and the issuance of threats against local officials, underscore themes Mr. Trump struck six years ago.

The 2020 election “seems to have been something of a catalyst” for their current actions, she added.

Mr. Trump built a powerhouse political movement by mobilizing supporters to align with his grievances, including his debunked claims of a conspiracy to steal the election and his rage over being prosecuted for his role in inciting the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

And the president has explicitly linked his stop-the-steal message six years ago to the midterm elections this year.

He exploded after a federal court recently rejected the department’s demand that officials in California stop counting 20,000 mail-in ballots over concerns the batch included noncitizens who voted illegally, even though such instances are exceedingly rare.

“Why would they reject fixing Election Fraud?” Mr. Trump wrote on social media on Saturday as he continued to stew over the Supreme Court’s refusal to consider his efforts to overturn the 2020 results.

“That’s like, in the 2020 Rigged and Stolen Election, when we had a great case, but the Supreme Court would not hear it because they said I, the President of the United States of America, had NO STANDING to bring such a case.”

This spring, Mr. Blanche, the president’s former defense lawyer, told Fox News that “there is a ton of evidence the election was rigged.” But he added that producing evidence that would hold up in court was “very difficult because they’re very good at hiding misconduct and hiding what they’re doing.”

Kiersten Pels, a Justice Department spokeswoman, dismissed the idea that the department’s actions in California and its effort to pre-emptively contest the results of the Alaska’s Senate race were impelled by any lingering grievances over 2020, just the determination to enforce laws the Biden administration would not.

“The Justice Department is focused on 2026 and on enforcing the federal laws that protect it,” Ms. Pels said. “Noncitizen voting is a federal crime. Prosecuting those cases is not ‘interceding’ in state elections. It is the job.”

If the department is facing criticism from the left for doing far too much, some on the right believe Mr. Blanche and his team are doing far too little.

Stephen K. Bannon, the former Trump aide who has long maintained that the 2020 election was stolen, said most of the department’s recent actions were aimed at keeping his boss happy, not at uncovering what he has said is a vast conspiracy to undermine Mr. Trump.

“Everything D.O.J. is doing is totally performative to give some patina of action,” he said in an interview. “Their heart isn’t in it. They slapped together a plan in the last 60 days after Trump started to really tune in.”

Several figures who played central roles in the post-2020 fight have emerged as influential voices in Mr. Trump’s ear. He recently met with Tina Peters, a former election official in Colorado who served prison time for breaching a county voting system. She has urged him to use the power of federal law enforcement to aggressively investigate elections without seeking court orders or the cooperation of state officials.

“He already has the authority to do all this — he doesn’t have to go to Congress to ask,” she told MS NOW on Monday. “If there’s something that is criminal in nature, he has every right to have the administration, the attorney general’s office or, you know, law enforcement go in and investigate.”

The assumptions undergirding the department’s two main lines of legal attack — the effort to sequester ballots based on contested assertions of illegal voting and the intervention, at Mr. Trump’s request, in the Alaska race — echo the drumbeat of 2020 election denialism.

“State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America,” Mr. Blanche said after suing California on Oct. 15. The move kicked off a period of litigation so intense that his tiny team of deputies has had to work around the clock to keep up with the demands of drafting the paperwork.

The effort, he added, was essential to “restore trust in American elections.”

Critics say it was aimed at achieving exactly the opposite, part of a determined political effort to undermine faith in elections — and one destined to fail in court.

“We’re seeing the same unsuccessful playbook as we did in 2020,” said Sam Oliker-Friedland, a former trial lawyer in the voting rights section of the department’s civil rights division. “It’s clear they haven’t learned that much.”

The federal judge in the California case, David O. Carter, rejected the department’s argument. He accused the administration of seeking to “disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.”

The department’s appeals in the case have thus far proved unsuccessful. On Monday, it petitioned the Supreme Court to uphold the suit.

The lawsuit embodied the evolution of the Trump administration’s strategy. It has shifted away from investigating broad-based claims of rampant voter fraud that William P. Barr, Mr. Trump’s attorney general during the 2020 election, dismissed as “completely bogus.”

Mr. Blanche and his team have coordinated closely with the Department of Homeland Security to target illegal voting by undocumented immigrants. That approach dovetails with the all-encompassing crackdown on immigration led by Mr. Trump’s top domestic adviser, Stephen Miller.

In the past nine weeks alone, the department has charged 192 immigrants across 26 states with illegal voting and registration offenses. Since the beginning of this administration, the department has charged 236 people with voting-fraud-related offenses, Ms. Pels said.

Another approach with shades of 2020 has been the department’s targeting of state and local election workers. Six years ago, Mr. Trump and his allies accused poll workers in Georgia and elsewhere of intentionally mishandling ballots. In October, the department sent warning letters and subpoenas to officials in California, accusing them of failing to comply with their demands.

On Friday, a federal judge in San Francisco ordered the department not to “threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials” based on the government’s suspicion a voter might be a noncitizen. She scheduled a hearing for Monday.

Mr. Blanche’s team has said its actions are necessary to safeguard the process. The flurry of 11th-hour activity, they have claimed, represents the urgency of addressing the threat posed by illegal voting with a goal of reminding local officials of their legal obligation to preserve records for future scrutiny.

Mr. Blanche has repeatedly offered assurances that the department’s recent activity was motivated by evidence, not politics. Last month, he told reporters the department would never “improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process.”

In the meantime, dodging questions about the 2020 election remains the go-to tactic of those seeking positions of power in the administration.

“Who won the 2020 election?” Senator Jon Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat, asked Jay Clayton, Mr. Trump’s nominee to be director of national intelligence, during his confirmation hearing in July.

“I’m not going to do this with you,” said Mr. Clayton, who was the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan before he was confirmed.

Mr. Ossoff persisted.

Mr. Clayton repeated that Mr. Biden had been certified the winner.

]]>

item.title: What Voters Should Know About Possible Problems at the Polls
item.description:
Americans will head to polling sites on Tuesday after a year in which President Trump has used the levers of the federal government to bolster unsubstantiated claims of election fraud.

Many election officials and Democrats have said they fear that the president’s attacks on the integrity of elections could lead to tensions as people vote, and to baseless challenges of the outcome. Local and state officials have even incorporated planning for potential federal intervention into their preparations for Election Day.

Nevertheless, it remains to be seen whether any worst-case scenarios will play out. And state and local authorities have emphasized that they are well prepared to help run a fair and safe election.

“The election officials in this country, the law enforcement in this country and other stakeholders are doing everything they possibly can to make sure that Election Day goes off without a hitch,” said Tina Barton, the co-chairwoman of the Committee for Safe and Secure Elections, an organization that has helped conduct election training sessions around the country. “Any incident that does happen is quickly mitigated because they already have a game plan for it.”

Here’s what voters should know:

Mr. Trump has notably refused to rule out invoking the Insurrection Act, in connection with the election. The 1807 law gives the president broad authority, under some conditions, to use the military to quell widespread domestic unrest. The extreme move has been encouraged by some of the president’s outside supporters.

In late August, however, the president’s top military adviser, Gen. Dan Caine, said there were no plans for the armed forces to deploy troops in relation to the elections. “I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections,” he wrote in a letter to a Democratic senator.

Legal experts say federal laws also prohibit troops or armed officials from being deployed to polling sites, even if Mr. Trump were to cite the Insurrection Act. “Federal law unambiguously prohibits the presence of armed federal officers at the polls, unless necessary to repel an armed attack by foreign enemies,” according to the Brennan Center for Justice.

Some voting rights advocates have also grown concerned about the prospect of Mr. Trump’s deploying Immigration and Customs Enforcement or other federal agents to polling sites. The Homeland Security Department has played a leading role in trying to find noncitizen voters to support the president’s false claims of widespread illegal voting.

But federal officials have downplayed that idea. Speaking to reporters in September, Markwayne Mullin, Mr. Trump’s homeland security secretary, said it was not the job of immigration agents to patrol polling places. He said they would be dispatched only “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down.”

Some election experts have noted that ICE agents are regularly dispatched on American streets as a part of their routine work, and that the mere sight of them near polling places could lead to misreporting on social media and cause fears among voters. They encourage members of the public to report concerns to poll workers or to election hotlines.

The Justice Department expects to have roughly 1,000 election monitors deployed in all 50 states on Election Day, according to Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the department’s civil rights unit. That is an expansion of past efforts, in which a smaller number monitors focused on states and city jurisdictions with a history of voting problems.

In an interview in August with Bloomberg, Ms. Dhillon said that the monitors would be deployed to places “where there may be language issues, the places where there may have been access of disability rights issues, places where there may be voter fraud issues that we’ve seen.”

The overall goal, she said, is “increasing all American citizens’ confidence in our elections.”

The large deployment by the Justice Department, which has promoted contested claims about election fraud and sought to preemptively challenge the results in the Alaska Senate race, has worried some local election officials. In recent days, some jurisdictions have issued statements saying that monitors are prohibited from crossing into an established perimeter surrounding polling locations, citing state law. Those laws vary by jurisdiction.

A Justice Department spokeswoman said that federal monitors did not require approval from state or local authorities, but added that monitors were trained to follow local laws that govern access at polling sites.

The Justice Department monitors will also not be authorized to make any arrests, a department lawyer said on Monday at a court hearing in Washington.

In nearly every place in the country, Justice Department monitors must follow the state regulations that apply to any visitors to polling places, including prohibitions on interfering with voters or intimidating them, said Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University who formerly worked as an adviser on voting rights in the Biden White House.

The rules are different for a separate category of federal observers, he added: monitors sent by the U.S. House of Representatives. Those observers have also been present at U.S. polling places for decades. Their job, according to the Committee on House Administration, which provides credentials to the observers, is to “ensure that conduct of the election was free and fair.”

Election machines are heavily monitored and regulated through testing and certification by federal agencies, states, local election offices and private labs.

In recent elections, however, rumors about “vote flipping,” in which voters’ choices are incorrectly logged, have gone viral on social media.

Election officials say that many of these problems are the result of user error. A recent examination of the issue by PolitiFact determined that “there is no evidence of voting machines deliberately designed with such flaws or that it is happening on a wide scale.”

“Historically, these types of rumors emerge from poorly designed or malfunctioning interfaces (and occasionally user error) but are often misleadingly framed as intentional attempts to switch votes instead of rare errors with remedies,” according to the Election Rumor Research team at the University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public.

Still, Mr. Trump and top administration officials have continuously promoted false claims that voting machines can be manipulated. Earlier this year, Mr. Mullin asked the Justice Department to examine whether a commonly used voting machine could be trusted. And Mr. Trump last month met with Tina Peters, a former Colorado county clerk who was convicted of tampering with voting machines after the 2020 election. Ms. Peters has called on Mr. Trump to inspect or seize voting machines — a move that legal experts say would be an overreach of federal authority.

Election experts said the public should be wary about any claims they see online about widespread irregularities with voting machines.

“It’s really important, first things first, for people to not spread unverified reports on social media about things that they’re seeing,” said Gowri Ramachandran, the director of elections and security at the Brennan Center for Justice. “It’s much better to, you know, let a poll worker know.”

Devlin Barrett and Eileen Sullivan contributed reporting.

]]>
